item.title: The Lindsay Clancy Case: Examining Postpartum Psychosis
item.description:
Postpartum Psychosis

The Lindsay Clancy Case: Examining Postpartum Psychosis

Personal Perspective: When the mental health system fails a postpartum mother.

Posted September 16, 2026

Key points
  • Lindsay Clancy allegedly suffered from postpartum psychosis.
  • Postpartum psychosis is a serious mental health disorder that, left untreated, can have fatal effects.
  • The mental health system appears to have failed Clancy in its treatment of her alleged postpartum psychosis.
Source: Anastas88/Megapixl.com

The Lindsay Clancy case recently ended in a mistrial where 11 jurors believed that she should be acquitted due to insanity based on the defense of postpartum psychosis. Therefore, with the jury deadlocked, Judge Sullivan declared a mistrial. The prosecution has yet to announce whether it will retry the case and there could be a new trial with a different jury. We will have to wait and see.

However, regardless of how one views the case, in all of its polarization, it sheds light on the very real phenomenon of postpartum psychosis and how the mental health system may be failing women suffering from this disorder.

Facts of the Lindsay Clancy case

In January of 2023, Lindsay Clancy, a wife, mother, and labor and delivery nurse, was accused of murdering her three children by strangulation and attempting to kill herself by jumping off her second-story balcony, leaving her paralyzed from the waist down. By all accounts, including her ex-husband Patrick, as well as colleagues, friends, and family, Lindsay was a dedicated mother who was extremely loving with her children. But sometime in 2022, Lindsay began showing signs of mental deterioration in the months leading up to the killings. Patrick testified that his ex-wife was struggling and began telling him that she was experiencing symptoms of extreme anxiety and depression. He stated that two months before the murders, Lindsay told him she was feeling suicidal and expressed thoughts of hurting the kids.

A chaplain who met with her following the killings reported that Lindsey allegedly heard a male voice telling her that if she didn't act, neither she nor her children would be safe. Further, her mother and sister testified that in the months leading up to the incident, she had become increasingly paranoid, with insomnia and suicidal thoughts. They further claimed that she became afraid to sleep alone and believed the numerous medications prescribed were worsening her mental health. In fact, Lindsay checked herself into Women & Infants Hospital of Rhode Island for treatment in December 2022 due to suicidal ideation but she was released the same day. She also attempted admission at another hospital but was rejected again.

Defense alleges mental health system failed Lindsay Clancy

The mental health system that Lindsay relied on appears to have failed her egregiously. It isn't that shocking, given that women's health, particularly mental health, is often characterized as females being dramatic or overly sensitive. We do this with mothers all the time. According to Hubert & Aujolat (2026), there is a moral high ground that we impose on women, expecting that if they feel overwhelmed, exhausted, depressed, or anxious, there is something inherently wrong with their ability to mother and this discourages them from seeking help. So they suffer in silence.

However, Lindsay Clancy did the opposite. She sought out treatment and braved the ridicule as a mother who was experiencing mental health deterioration. Her doctors allegedly misdiagnosed her bipolar disorder with postpartum onset and subjected her to a disorganised, uncoordinated course of pharmacology that may have made her anxiety, depression, and ideation worsen and eventually led to what her lawyers called a severe psychotic break.

Lindsay's care was described by her attorney as disjointed while she was being dangerously overmedicated with no continuity of care. Further, when she attempted to check herself into the hospital, she was let go the same day and denied care at another facility. This was weeks before she allegedly killed her children and attempted to end her own life.

Postpartum psychosis

According to Michalczyk, Mitosz, and Soroka (2023), while postpartum psychosis is rare, it is a serious clinical affliction that is still not in the DSM. Bergink (2026) defines postpartum psychosis, or PP, as a severe psychiatric illness with onset within weeks after delivery and a high risk of suicide and infanticide. Bergink asserts that PP is an acute and severe episode of psychosis, mania, or depression after childbirth. It occurs after 0.1% to .02 % of deliveries in women without a mental illness history (2026). Most women with PP experience severe mood symptoms, including mania, mixed episodes, or depression with psychotic features. Bergink further explains that impaired cognition, irritability, and agitation are also typical. Moreover, there is overlap between PP and bipolar disorder (2026). The specific timing of PP strongly suggests a biological basis, because the postpartum period is signified by endocrine, immune, and neuroanatomical and physiological changes in the brain (2026). It is thought to have a genetic basis, and the significant hormonal and immune fluctuations that occur after delivery likely trigger the disorder (2026).

Bergink argues that PP is a psychiatric emergency and often requires hospitalization of the mother to avoid deadly possibilities. However, if detected and addressed in time, PP responds well to treatment and most women return to their premorbid functioning (2026). PP seems to respond well to a stepwise sequence of short-term benzodiazepines, antipsychotics, and lithium combined with electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) if needed, with a 98% reduction rate for patients who are hospitalized (2026). If left untreated, PP is known to potentially have tragic outcomes with maternal suicide and infanticide.

Lindsay Clancy turned to the mental health system for help. However, she may have been left to handle her symptoms of postpartum psychosis alone. She allegedly had multiple doctors prescribing various medications with no continuity of care compounded with a misdiagnosis of bipolar disorder. Her defense team argued her doctors didn't coordinate with each other or check in on Lindsay to see the effects that the medicines were having.

Further, she attempted to be admitted to the hospital, which is the standard protocol for postpartum psychosis, and she was turned away. Lindsay was then allegedly denied access to yet another facility. She tried to get help and at every turn was dismissed. The 11 jurors who voted for her acquittal are likely a testament to her attorney's claim that the mental health system deeply failed Lindsey and her children.

item.title: Are You Too "Busy" to Connect?
item.description:
Relationships

Are You Too "Busy" to Connect?

How that overbooked social calendar impacts our happiness.

Posted September 16, 2026

Key points
  • Being around people isn't the same as truly making connections.
  • Research on loneliness suggests that showing up isn't what matters, it's whether you feel like you belong.
  • Four questions can help you figure out if you have deep relationships.
  • We have the ability to impact our happiness through our everyday actions with others.

Okay, so don’t look now, but if you had to guess, how many social events do you have on your calendar for this week?

Maybe you’ve calendared your workouts twice a week with a friend or penciled in coffee with a neighbor. Do you go to book clubs religiously? On paper, you look “busy,” but here is the million-dollar question: Does going to all of the activities on your calendar really make you feel more connected?

That’s the problem; it’s common to confuse being booked with being connected. Just because you’re filling up that calendar doesn’t mean you’re not struggling with loneliness. It’s confusing because we are around others and talking to people, but that doesn’t always translate to true connection.

The thing is, science tells us that just being in the presence of others doesn’t give us the result we’re looking for. If you spend a lot of time with people and still feel like you don’t know people, this post is for you.

We can look at the research on loneliness to help us navigate this issue. In a study from Barcelona, Spain, researchers looked at 320 adults who reported high levels of loneliness to understand it further. In the study, half of the group participated in organized outdoor group sessions that focused on helping people build relationships. The other half of the group was just given information about local activities and told to join them on their own.

The results showed that after only three months, the first group showed real benefits. They reported a sense of belonging to the group, started trusting group members, and were more comfortable trying new things together. The second group just reported on the number of events that they participated in during the timeframe.

The thing is, there's nuance because the outcomes cannot be measured just in terms of attendance at events on the calendar. The data clearly shows that even if you attend every meeting, you can still feel lonely.

So, What Makes a Relationship Matter?

According to the U.S. Surgeon General’s Connection Advisory report, there are three important aspects of creating healthy, connected relationships.

Structure: Do you have people in your life? Do you truly spend time with people?

Support: If something happens, is there someone you would call?

Quality: When you're with people, can you be your true, authentic self?

Structure is easy to track because you can actually count the numbers: the people you spend time with, the invitations you accept, and what your calendar looks like. In the evaluation world, these are called outputs rather than outcomes.

Support and quality are a little more difficult to measure, and they are also more important for developing connections. So, here are four questions you can ask yourself to help determine if you are truly connecting in your life or if you need to focus on this a bit more:

1. If something happened, who would I call at 11:00 PM?

This is not about your contact list or how many friends you have on social media; we want to know who you would call if you were having a rough night and needed to talk.

We’re not judging; we’re just looking for information. If you can’t identify someone, that is important information for you about your connections. It may mean that you need to focus less on meeting new people or those “weak” ties and focus more on building deeper relationships. We want “strong” ties to fill this need.

2. Who can I be my true authentic self around?

It’s nice to be popular and included in many events, but where do you feel like you truly belong? We feel like we belong when we are with people who know us well enough so that we can relax and be ourselves. You feel you can be yourself when you don't have to be “on” or put on a performance, and it's okay if you feel like being quiet. In spaces where you truly belong, you feel comfortable disagreeing or admitting when you are having a rough time.

Now take a minute to think about the people or places where you feel like you belong. If nothing comes to mind, that’s more information for you about a need in your life.

3. When you spend time with someone, how do you feel afterwards?

You just had a nice meal with friends, and when you leave, there’s a smile on your face, or maybe you feel lighter or energized; those are your people. In contrast, maybe you leave the meal and you are drained, exhausted, or feeling insecure; these relationships are taking energy away from you.

Take a minute to identify the people who make you feel energized and those who don’t. Who are you spending more time with?

4. Ask yourself if the relationship has changed you in some way.

The thing is that real relationships typically go somewhere; meaning you try new things or get honest with yourself about something that you learned from them. Secure relationships make you feel more confident, and you can feel open to talking about your hopes and dreams.

Not every relationship is going to be transformational, but if you have known someone for years and have never moved past small talk, your relationship may be more about habit or routine than true connection.

If You’re Feeling Lonely, You Need Fewer Activities and More Connection

So, like many of you, my calendar looks full, and the more hectic I am, the less connected I feel. When I’m traveling a lot for work, I miss the monthly book club or walking three times a week in the evening with a friend. When I am feeling this way, I must be intentional about focusing on one relationship at a time and being present (without the phone) for the time that we are together.

I recently reconnected with an old friend, and we committed to walking together once a week. I can honestly say that now I am looking forward to those walks, and pretty quickly we rekindled our friendship from 15 years ago. I noticed that this one relationship ended up doing more for my sense of connection and belonging than the “busy” events on my calendar.

What’s the takeaway? My lesson is that I don’t need more groups to join, more invitations to events, or more activities. I just needed one or two relationships where I can be honest, feel understood, and build trust.

I’m not saying quit your book club; we need those too. What I’m saying is don’t use that attendance as proof of connection. The question isn't “how often am I around people?”, but rather, “who do I feel like I belong with?” Because belonging is what real connection is all about!

item.title: 5 Reasons We Still Judge Women Who Date Younger Men
item.description:
Relationships

5 Reasons We Still Judge Women Who Date Younger Men

The age-gap relationship double standard we have yet to outgrow.

Posted September 16, 2026

Key points
  • Not every age-gap relationship is created the same.
  • The assumption is often that the younger partner must have “mommy issues” or “daddy issues."
  • A predominant belief is that women become less desirable as they age, while men may become more desirable.
  • When our relationships are recognized by the people around us, it can strengthen the bond between partners.
Source: Dmytro Zinkevych / Shutterstock

Age-gap relationships face challenges that their same-age counterparts do not. For example, partners may have different levels of emotional maturity and energy, may be at different stages in their careers, or have different financial circumstances or social and professional networks. Later stages of life can come with responsibilities to children from previous relationships or having to take care of aging parents. In addition, an age difference can also result in different ideas of fun. One person may want to go to every music festival on the planet, while the other person may be perfectly fine binge-watching reruns of Friends every weekend.

These are legitimate dilemmas that couples may need to manage together. They don't, however, automatically make a relationship unhealthy.

One of the complications of age-gap relationships is that they come with a cultural assumption that to be attracted to someone older, the younger partner must have “mommy issues” or “daddy issues.”

As much as age-gap relationships may be subject to scrutiny and judgment, the truth is that not every age-gap relationship is created the same.

An older man with a younger woman may get an eye roll, but we get the script. When an older woman is with a younger man, however, everyone seems to feel entitled to offer their unsolicited opinions. Why is this?

1. Women’s Desirability Comes With an Earlier Expiration Date

A predominant cultural belief is that women become less desirable as they age, while men, especially if they're driving the right car, may become even more desirable.

A 55-year-old man dating a 35-year-old woman might be accused of having a midlife crisis, but even that stereotype comes with an approving wink. He gets a beautiful younger woman on his arm, while she gets a new wardrobe, spa weekends, and meals at top-notch restaurants. It’s considered transactional.

A 52-year-old woman dating a 30-year-old man doesn’t get the same wink. She’s referred to as a cougar, which is far from kind. It defines the woman as the pursuer and the younger man as her prey.

From the endless products sold to women to preserve their youth, the clear message is that women are not supposed to age. Once we're wrinkled and gray, we're expected to bake cookies for the grandchildren, not reevaluate our lives or fall in love again. Women are not granted the same rights as men to finally do the things they’ve always wanted to do or immerse themselves fully in the freedom that comes in later stages of life.

2. He Can’t Possibly Find Her Hot

When the younger partner is a woman, she may be subjected to another sexist stereotype, that of the gold digger. The assumption may be that she’s after money, security, or status.

Yet, when the younger partner is a man, the social script gets even more complicated. Younger men can be perceived as gold diggers too, but that is a notion we judge more harshly. Being financially inferior to a woman may challenge traditional standards of masculinity. Men are expected to be providers, and their worth is often tied to their bank accounts. For that reason, younger male partners labeled as gold diggers may be perceived as more damaged.

3. We Assume the Older Partner Holds the Cards and We Don't Like When It's Her

Age differences can create power imbalances. One partner may control the finances, own the home, have a more high-stakes career, or possess a much wider professional or social network. These differences can become problematic when they are used to manipulate or diminish the other person's autonomy.

However, age alone doesn't tell us who holds the power. The younger partner may very well earn more money, have greater social capital, have more sexual or relationship experience, possess greater confidence, or be more dominant in the relationship.

Power in relationships can come from money, status, beauty, professional influence, emotional leverage, family resources, caregiving, citizenship, housing, or who is more afraid of losing whom.

4. We Assume the Same Life Stage Means Compatibility

As a couples therapist, I have witnessed repeatedly that the number of birthday candles on a cake does not predict compatibility.

Over the years, I have worked with couples close in age who cannot stand one another and also couples with significant age differences who genuinely enjoy each other's company.

Chronological age certainly positions us in life. It can influence our experiences, priorities, responsibilities, and goals. However, it doesn't reliably predict emotional maturity, attachment patterns, shared values, sexual compatibility, curiosity, humor, or readiness for commitment.

Two people can be 32 and want completely different lives. A 34-year-old and a 54-year-old can be on the same page about their lifestyle and values.

In fact, choosing a relationship that falls outside conventional expectations may require more willingness and intentionality. When people know that their relationship will be interrogated, they may be forced to have difficult conversations at early stages of their relationship and may have arrived at a consensus about where they are heading.

And of course, deliberately and knowingly choosing each other doesn't guarantee happily ever after, but nothing does.

5. We Treat Her Aging Like a Ticking Clock

What about children?

If a woman is of reproductive age, she’s expected to marry someone ready to pursue this task with her, and since our general theory is that men mature later, it can’t be a younger man.

And of course, it definitely can't be that she just doesn’t want kids.

Fertility can be a very real challenge in an age-gap relationship. If a younger man wants biological children and his older female partner is approaching the end of her reproductive years, great chemistry may still not be enough to resolve this conflict. Couples need to talk about whether their visions for a family are compatible and what options they would consider.

The thing is that fertility isn't just an "older woman problem." People of the same age can discover that they have very different timelines for having children, experience infertility, change their minds about parenthood, or disagree about whether they want children at all.

The same is true of the other concerns that come with a significant age difference. Health, caregiving, retirement, sexual functioning, and lifestyle may eventually require difficult conversations. Also, same-age couples are not immune to the unpredictability and chaos of life.

People become ill, experience libido changes, go through unpredictable career transitions, get divorced two months into a marriage, and sometimes die young.

We tolerate enormous uncertainty in relationships but still perceive an older woman's aging as a foreseeable threat.

Humans are creatures of connection. We desperately want to belong and feel accepted and appreciated within our communities. When our relationships are recognized by the people around us, that sense of fitting in can strengthen the bond between partners. In contrast, a relationship that is repeatedly questioned or judged is compromised. Perhaps the greatest threat to any relationship is our insistence that it needs to be approved by others.
